## How to use this

The code from Lecture 23, run, with the numbers it produces, and the habitat
exercise solved.

. . .

`lm()` gives exact answers, so your numbers should match these. The recipe's
draws are random, so those may differ in the last decimal place.

::: {.notes}
Posted after class so nobody is left wondering whether their answer was right.
:::

## Setting up {.smaller}

```{r}
library(bbmle)
library(biometrydata)

songbirds <- avonet[avonet$Order1 == "Passeriformes", ]
birds <- data.frame(species = songbirds$Species1,
                    family = songbirds$Family1,
                    hwi = songbirds$Hand.Wing.Index,
                    lat = abs(songbirds$Centroid.Latitude),
                    migration_code = songbirds$Migration,
                    habitat_code = songbirds$Habitat.Density)
birds <- na.omit(birds)
nrow(birds)
```

## Regression, two ways {.smaller}

```{r}
m_lat <- mle2(hwi ~ dnorm(mean = a + b * lat, sd = s),
              start = list(a = 15, b = 0, s = 5), data = birds)
lm_lat <- lm(hwi ~ lat, data = birds)

coef(m_lat)
coef(lm_lat)
c(logLik(m_lat), logLik(lm_lat))
```

## Reading the fit {.smaller}

```{r}
summary(lm_lat)
confint(lm_lat)
sigma(lm_lat)
```

## The number trap {.smaller}

```{r}
lm_num <- lm(hwi ~ migration_code, data = birds)
coef(lm_num)

birds$migration <- factor(birds$migration_code, levels = 1:3,
                          labels = c("sedentary", "partial", "migratory"))
lm_mig <- lm(hwi ~ migration, data = birds)
coef(lm_mig)
coef(lm(hwi ~ migration - 1, data = birds))
AIC(lm_num, lm_mig)
```

## Latitude and migration together {.smaller}

```{r}
lm_add <- lm(hwi ~ lat + migration, data = birds)
lm_int <- lm(hwi ~ lat * migration, data = birds)

AICtab(lm_lat, lm_mig, lm_add, lm_int)
coef(lm_add)
confint(lm_add)
```

## Are the assumptions met? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 8
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(lm_add, which = 2)
plot(lm_add, which = 1)
```

## Who is in the long tail? {.smaller}

```{r}
# average residual by family: how much more pointed than predicted
head(sort(tapply(resid(lm_add), birds$family, mean), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

# one fix: model log(hwi), which pulls in the long upper tail
lm_log <- lm(log(hwi) ~ lat + migration, data = birds)
```

Swallows (Hirundinidae) catch insects on the wing, and their wings are far more
pointed than the model expects.

## On the log scale {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 5
plot(lm_log, which = 2)
```

Much closer to the line, with the long upper tail gone. Thursday's generalized
linear models are the other route.

## Intervals, the quick way {.smaller}

```{r}
new_bird <- data.frame(lat = 45,
                       migration = factor("migratory", levels = levels(birds$migration)))

predict(lm_add, newdata = new_bird, interval = "confidence")
predict(lm_add, newdata = new_bird, interval = "prediction")
```

## The same intervals, by Lecture 21's recipe {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(23)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(1000, mu = coef(lm_add), Sigma = vcov(lm_add))

# the mean for a migratory bird at 45 degrees, for each draw
mu_draws <- draws[, "(Intercept)"] + draws[, "lat"] * 45 + draws[, "migrationmigratory"]
quantile(mu_draws, c(0.025, 0.975))

# add the scatter of one new species
quantile(rnorm(1000, mean = mu_draws, sd = sigma(lm_add)), c(0.025, 0.975))
```

## Drawing the predictions {.smaller}

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

grid <- expand.grid(lat = 0:70, migration = levels(birds$migration))
conf <- predict(lm_add, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence")
pred <- predict(lm_add, newdata = grid, interval = "prediction")
grid <- data.frame(grid, conf, pred_lwr = pred[, "lwr"], pred_upr = pred[, "upr"])
head(grid, 3)
```

## The figure {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
ggplot(grid, aes(x = lat)) +
  geom_point(data = birds, aes(y = hwi), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pred_lwr, ymax = pred_upr), fill = "#2a7ab0", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "#2a7ab0", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit)) +
  facet_wrap(~ migration) +
  labs(x = "degrees from the equator", y = "hand-wing index")
```

## Does the model match the data? {.smaller}

```{r}
# each species' own prediction interval
pi_data <- predict(lm_add, newdata = birds, interval = "prediction")
inside <- birds$hwi > pi_data[, "lwr"] & birds$hwi < pi_data[, "upr"]

mean(inside)                                           # share inside: about 0.95?
mean(birds$hwi[!inside] > pi_data[!inside, "upr"])     # share of misses above
```

Close to 95% inside, but nearly all the misses are above the band: the
band is symmetric and the data have a long upper tail, as the Q-Q plot showed.

## Good enough? {.smaller}

```{r}
exp(confint(lm_log))   # each effect is now "times"
exp(predict(lm_log, newdata = new_bird, interval = "prediction"))
predict(lm_add, newdata = new_bird, interval = "prediction")
```

Migrants still have more pointed wings, and latitude still points the same way.
What changes is the prediction for one new species: the log model's interval
reaches much higher, where the swallows are.

## Your turn: habitat {.smaller}

```{r}
lm_hab_num <- lm(hwi ~ lat + migration + habitat_code, data = birds)

birds$habitat <- factor(birds$habitat_code, levels = 1:3,
                        labels = c("dense", "semi-open", "open"))
lm_hab_fac <- lm(hwi ~ lat + migration + habitat, data = birds)

AICtab(lm_add, lm_hab_num, lm_hab_fac)
confint(lm_hab_fac)
```

## Your turn, in biology {.smaller}

Habitat matters on top of migration and latitude, and it has to go in as a
factor: forest and semi-open songbirds differ by only
`r sprintf("%.1f", coef(lm_hab_fac)["habitatsemi-open"])` HWI points, while
open-country songbirds have wings about
`r sprintf("%.1f", coef(lm_hab_fac)["habitatopen"])` points more pointed than forest
birds. The numeric version forces those two steps to be equal.

## For anyone fast {.smaller}

```{r}
# does the habitat effect depend on migration?
lm_hab_int <- lm(hwi ~ lat + migration * habitat, data = birds)

# is the latitude effect curved?
lm_quad <- lm(hwi ~ lat + I(lat^2) + migration, data = birds)

AICtab(lm_hab_fac, lm_hab_int)
AICtab(lm_add, lm_quad)
coef(lm_quad)
```

Both help. The squared term is positive: wings change little across the tropics
and become more pointed beyond them.
